newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile-Canada trade deal in limbo, awaiting key vote.
newsitem.headline: Chile-Canada trade deal in limbo, awaiting key vote.

text.p: A free trade agreement between Chile and Canada due to go into effect on Tuesday will be delayed at least a few days because the Chilean Senate has yet to ratify it, diplomatic sources said on Monday.

The treaty, intended to sweep away tariffs on most trade between the two countries starting on Tuesday, will stay in limbo until President Eduardo Frei's government is sure it has the votes in the Senate to pass it, the sources said.
The Senate was expected to approve the deal on Wednesday, allowing it to take effect on Thursday.
"The ratification process is taking a bit longer than we expected," said one Canadian diplomatic source. "Obviously Canada's interest is that it be approved so it can take effect."
The treaty will erase tariffs on about 80 percent of trade between the two countries upon implementation and phase out the rest over the next 18 years.
It has met opposition from legislators from grain and dairy regions in southern Chile, where farmers say they will be hurt by Canadian imports.

The farmers were still smarting from Chile's signing of a free trade deal with the four-nation Mercosur bloc last year, which they said would flood Chile with cheap Argentine and Brazilian grain, and said the Canadian deal will worsen their plight.

But the treaty passed overwhelmingly in the Chamber of Deputies by a 78-21 vote, and a Senate committee recommended passage of it by 10-4 in mid-June. Supporters said they are confident of ratification.

"It would be unthinkable for the Senate to approve the earlier treaty (with Mercosur) and then not approve this one, since its benefits outweigh the costs," said well-known economist Vittorio Corbo, quoted in the Santiago daily La Segunda. "There will be some losers in the short term but the country will come out ahead."
The treaty was initialed by President Eduardo Frei and Prime Minister Jean Chretien in Ottawa on Nov. 18, and later signed by their countries' top trade officials.

Both governments say it will help pave the way for Chile eventually to join the North American Free Trade Agreement because its terms closely mirror those of NAFTA -- so much so that it has been dubbed "NAFTA Light."
Chile already has a free trade pact with the third NAFTA partner, Mexico, leaving only the United States left to negotiate a tariff reduction agreement with Latin America's most prosperous nation.

The Canada treaty was originally supposed to go into effect on June 1. Implementation was delayed a month at Chile's request to give the Senate time to vote on it, and Chile would have to ask for another delay if more than a few days go by without a vote, the sources said.
